course_name_original: Kaos Teorisi ve Doğrusal Olmayan Dinamiklere Giriş
course_name_en: Introduction to Chaos Theory and Nonlinear Dynamics

learning_outcomes.text: Define and apply advanced Electrical-Electronics Engineering concepts.
Formulate and solve advanced engineering problems.
Outline, examine, and work on project details from an Electrical and Electronics Engineering perspective.
Carefully review the literature in line with the research project and connect their own results with previous literature.
Design and conduct independent research projects.
Work effectively in research teams with interdisciplinary interactions.
Develop continuous learning awareness with modern technology.
Find methods to improve existing knowledge.

syllabus_topics: Introduction to chaos theory and nonlinear dynamics; deterministic systems, complex behavior, and engineering motivation.
Mathematical fundamental concepts: state variables, phase space, autonomous systems, concepts of orbit and flow.
Equilibrium points, linearization, local stability, and phase plane interpretation.
Discrete-time systems and one-dimensional maps; logistic map and iteration logic.
Periodic orbits, cobweb diagrams, and transition to chaos via period-doubling.
Basic bifurcation types: saddle-node, transcritical, pitchfork, and period-doubling bifurcations.
Phase portraits in continuous-time nonlinear systems; Poincaré-Bendixson theorem and limit cycles.
Classical chaotic systems: Lorenz system, Rössler system, and fundamental dynamic properties.
Sensitivity to initial conditions and Lyapunov exponents; basic calculation and interpretation.
Strange attractors, fractal structure, fractal dimension, and geometric interpretation of chaotic attractors.
Poincaré sections, return maps, and basic numerical indicators used in chaos detection.
Examples of nonlinear behavior in electrical-electronics engineering; circuits, control systems, and oscillations.
Introduction to chaos-based applications: synchronization, secure communication, control, and engineering applications.
General review; example system analyses, student work, and evaluation of in-term applications.
